title: What the homepage has to prove for a restaurant group
metaTitle: What a restaurant group homepage must prove
excerpt: A restaurant group homepage should show the room and one dish, then offer the menu or a table. A logo animation fails a guest who is deciding where to go tonight.
alt: Yellow California poppies against a clear blue sky, a bright first impression that still has to point a hungry guest toward one real room.
caption: A clear sky and a single kind of flower. The first screen should be that direct. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should the first screen of a restaurant group site show?
faqs.answer: The room and one dish, plus a way to see the menu or book a table. If you run several restaurants, the first screen should help a guest pick one for tonight, with the neighborhood or the hours visible. A logo drawing itself does not answer where to go.

faqs.question: How do we feature more than one restaurant?
faqs.answer: Give each room a name, a place, and one picture a guest can tell apart. Lead with the one that best explains the group, then list the others as choices, not as equal abstract tiles. A guest should be able to say which room they are booking before they hit the button.

faqs.question: Where do hours and location belong?
faqs.answer: On the first screen or one tap from it, as text. A guest deciding tonight will not open a PDF or wait for a map tile. Repeat hours on the restaurant they chose. A group homepage that hides Tuesday's closure will create a bad walk.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A restaurant group homepage has one job for a guest deciding where to go tonight: show the room and one dish, and offer a way to see the menu or book a table. A logo animation fails that guest. They are not waiting to be introduced to a holding company. They are hungry, or they are texting a friend, and they need a room they can picture.

Write the page in that order. The room. One dish that tells the cooking. The menu or the booking. Everything else can wait until those three are obvious.

## Tonight, not the group chart

The reader is rarely studying your corporate structure. They are choosing dinner. The page should assume that and answer it. Which room. What it feels like. What a plate looks like. Whether they can still get in.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that people often leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and that a clear value proposition in the first 10 seconds earns a longer look. For this guest the value proposition is a place they might sit tonight. A film about the founders spends those seconds on a story they did not ask for.

[Google's helpful content guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has a primary purpose for people who might come to you directly. The purpose is to help someone pick a restaurant and move toward a menu or a table. A page built to impress other restaurateurs, or to premiere a rebrand, misses the person on the sidewalk.

If you have one flagship and two siblings, say so in the layout. Lead with the room a stranger should understand first. Do not give four venues equal mystery. Equality in the grid is how nobody gets chosen.

Name the neighborhood in the first screen. A beautiful room in the wrong part of town is a different decision from a beautiful room nearby. The guest should not have to open a map to learn the basic fact.

## The room and one dish

Show a photograph of the room as a guest will see it: tables, light, the distance between seats, something that tells them if this is a loud counter or a quiet booth. Then show one dish, plated as it leaves the pass, not a collage and not a logo stamped on a napkin.

The dish is doing explanatory work. A bowl of noodles, a chop, a slice of pie. It should be specific enough that a person can taste the promise. If the restaurants cook differently, do not use one generic "food" image for the group. Use the dish from the room you are featuring, and label which restaurant it belongs to.

Write one sentence under each picture. "The front room at dusk, twenty-four seats, walk-ins when we can." "The grilled leek, which is on the dinner menu at this restaurant." Captions are how the pictures become a decision. Without them, you have a mood.

Skip the logo animation entirely on this page. It delays the room. It also trains the team to think the brand mark is the product. The product is dinner. The mark can sit in the header, small, and stay still.

If a restaurant is closed tonight, do not lead with it. Lead with one that is open, and say the hours in text. A guest who crosses town for a dark door will not blame the photograph. They will blame the site.

## A way to the menu or a table

The action is practical. See the menu, or book a table. If both matter, put both on the first screen as text buttons, and make clear which restaurant they apply to. A single "Reserve" that dumps a guest into the wrong venue is worse than a short list.

Use the booking tool you actually use. A deep link to the right venue, the right party size if you know it, and tonight's service. Do not build a fake reservation widget that emails the office and hopes. If the books are kept in a known system, send the guest there with the restaurant already selected.

The menu should open on a phone without a dance. HTML that you can update is better than a PDF that fails. If you must use a PDF this week, test it on a phone before you link it from the hero. A menu that does not open is a closed restaurant.

Repeat the action after the list of rooms. A guest who scrolls to compare should not lose the button. Keep the words stable. "Menu" and "Book a table." Not "Embark" and "Join us."

Say what the button will not do. Booking a table for two is not a buyout. If private dining is a different path, give it a text link, not the primary button. The homepage is for tonight's guest first.

## Several restaurants, one choice

When the group has multiple rooms, the homepage is a chooser. Each choice needs:

- The name a local would say.
- The neighborhood.
- One sentence on what dinner there is like.
- The room or the dish.
- Hours for today, or a clear weekly line.
- Menu and book, already aimed at that room.

Four lines and a picture. Then the next restaurant. A guest should be able to compare without learning your internal brand architecture.

If the rooms share a kitchen style, say the shared idea once, in a sentence, then let the rooms differ. "Wood fire, three rooms" is enough group story for the first screen. The essay about sourcing can live on an about page for the guest who wants it after they have picked.

Do not force a personality quiz, a city map with tiny pins, or a horizontal swipe as the only index. Stack the choices. Name them in text. Pins can support the list. They should not replace it.

A new restaurant that is not open yet should be marked as such. "Opens in spring" with no date you will regret, or with a mailing line that is clearly not a booking. Do not let it take the hero from a room that is serving tonight.

## What the logo animation costs

The animation feels like craft in a design review. On the street it is a lock screen. The guest waits, or they tap Skip and feel flicked away, and they still have not seen a chair or a plate.

It also hides whether the site is fast. A heavy intro often means the real page loads late. The guest needed hours and a dish. They got a drawing of a monogram. That is the failure mode for this buyer. Cut it. If the motion is a two-frame settle of the header, and the room is already visible, you are fine. If the room is behind the animation, you are not.

The same cut applies to a full-screen video of hands and steam with no venue name. Steam is not a neighborhood. Put the film lower, muted, with a caption, after the guest knows where they are.

Look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) when you need a reference for pages that put a real subject first and a mark second. Hanabi designs and builds marketing sites in that order. The homepage can be beautiful and still lead with the room. Beauty that postpones dinner is the animation's problem, not beauty itself.

## Order, then stop

A practical order:

1. One open restaurant: room, dish, neighborhood, hours.
2. Menu and book for that restaurant.
3. The other rooms, each with the same facts, shorter.
4. A line on private dining, only if it is real, linked onward.
5. A short line on who cooks, linked to the about page, not a biography.

Then stop. Press quotes can sit under the room they refer to. A group manifesto can sit elsewhere. The homepage is the decision.

Check it on a phone in the evening, outside, with one thumb. Can you tell where to go and how to book before the screen dims? If you have to wait for type to fade in, change the build. Next.js can serve this as a straightforward page. The craft is the crop and the sentence, not a timeline.

Update hours when they change. A homepage that lies about Monday is a trust problem no dish can fix. Make hours a field someone on the floor can correct. Do not bury them in a designed image.

Read the first screen to someone who has never been to the restaurants. Ask which room they would book, and for what kind of night. If they cannot answer, the pictures are still a mood. Add the neighborhood, the seat count or the counter, and the dish name until they can. That test is faster than another round of animation. Do it before you add a press logo or a second film. The guest tonight will not award you points for completeness. They will award you the booking, or they will keep scrolling to someone who showed a chair.

## The price they will ask anyway

Once the room is convincing, many guests still hesitate for a plain reason. They do not know if dinner is a splurge, a normal night, or a set menu they must commit to. They will ask the host if the site will not say. The next page is where that shape lives, without turning the group into a software pricing table.

Read [a pricing page for a restaurant group](/blog/a-pricing-page-for-a-restaurant-group) when the homepage shows the room and the check still feels like a secret. The guest is judging fit. Give them the shape before they book the wrong night.
